title: How fast things vanish
hookLine: how quickly all things disappear, bodies and memories alike (Meditations 2.12)

cards: A corner store becomes a phone shop. A teacher retires and moves away. The song everyone hummed one summer stops being played.
Far enough back in an old photo album, there are faces nobody in the family can name. It happens so gradually that it only shows when someone looks back.
In section twelve, Marcus looks back, and looks hard, and starts with a sentence that's almost a sigh.

teach.b: First, two kinds of vanishing. How quickly everything disappears, Marcus says: bodies, out of the world, and then the memory of them, out of time. First the person goes.
Then, more slowly, the remembering goes.
Second, what dazzles. Then he looks at the things that pull hardest: things that tempt with pleasure, things that frighten with pain, things people brag about.
How cheap they are, he says, how perishable, how quickly gone. It's the same trick this path met with the emperor's purple robe: looking at something until its glamour wears off. Third, death itself.

Looked at alone, he says, stripped of all the imaginings piled onto it, dying is simply a work of nature. And to be terrified of a work of nature is, in his words, to be like a child. He doesn't mean grief is childish.
He means the dread added on top of the plain fact.

teach.h: HOW DO WE COME NEAR TO GOD?
teach.b: Fourth, what's near. The entry ends by pointing at something to look into, not an answer: how a human being comes near to God, by what part of himself, and when.
He doesn't name the part here; a few days ago you met the one he calls the ruling part. Readers on other paths will name it differently, or not at all. But the turn is worth noticing.
After everything that vanishes, he points at what's closest. Not to escape the vanishing.
To stand in it, steadily, and say: so quickly. And then, still, to live today.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism reflect regularly on impermanence, letting it loosen the grip of status and pleasure and sharpen their attention to the present.

games.q: what does “how fast things vanish” mean?
o: bodies, then their memory, pass quickly from the world
regret over hours wasted on things that didn't matter
how the empire's wealth was spent on foolish wars

games.q: how fast things vanish — tap the pairs.
p: by what part we come near God

s: he calls the dread we pile onto death childish, not grief.
Marcus calls death, looked at plainly, a work of nature
strip away the imaginings and that's what's left.
Marcus says only bodies vanish, but memories last forever
first the bodies go, then the memory of them.

games.q: you look through old photos and feel a wave of dread at how fast it all goes. what does Meditations 2.12 suggest?
o: look plainly: it's nature's work; strip off the added dread.
take more photos so nothing is lost.
games.why: look at it alone, Marcus says, without the imaginings, and you'll see a work of nature.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that's already gone, a place, a voice, a version of yourself from ten years ago, and see it clearly for a moment, noticing how quickly it went and how it still lives a little in you.
Then come back to this breath, which is also going, and is still here.

wordCard.voice: How fast things vanish. Marcus: bodies leave the world, and then their memory leaves time, so quickly. Death, seen plainly, is a work of nature. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: nature. For Marcus, dying is 'a work of nature', nothing more frightening than that.

carryVoice: Your line: so quickly. A mug, a face, the light: here now, and worth enjoying. See you tomorrow.
